summaries.summary: Typical single-domain dialog systems store flat data in relational databases, enabling efficient queries and slot-based dialog state tracking with probabilistic belief tracking.
The well-defined database structure of typical dialog systems is costly to extend because new information must fit the format, especially for new domains.
Knowledge-base dialog systems offer flexible knowledge graphs and access to large growing resources such as Freebase and Wikidata.
The paper proposes a dataset for developing and evaluating knowledge-base dialog systems by interactive learning and outlines the remaining sections.
For dialog systems providing general information from a knowledge base, poor understanding of many questions is the most limiting factor.
Current approaches achieve around 50% accuracy on some question answering datasets, motivating interactive learning from dialogs through additional user information.
Interactive learning can obtain correct answers, broader explanations, improved policies, and rephrasing from users to improve dialog systems.
The collected dataset mainly enables the proposed interactive learning steps and potentially evaluates how different systems perform on this task.
Identifying the information users want is difficult for knowledge-graph dialog systems, but dialog systems can ask for additional information.
The authors distinguish three different basic approaches to requesting knowledge bases.
Combinations of approaches are possible, and the authors collected a dataset to fill the gap in public datasets for interactive learning.
Offline evaluation of interactive dialogs is difficult, so data were collected to simulate all dialog variants possible according to any policy.
The considered dialog variants differ only in the presence of several parts, allowing collection of dialogs containing all interactive learning information.
The dataset enables simulation where the policy decides how much extra information to request, including explanations, answers, or rerouting to another user.
Simulated user answers can be incorrect because human users made mistakes, and these mistakes are intentionally kept in the dataset.
A perfect data collection scenario would use a real running dialog system with real users to request explanations and answers.
Because access to systems with real users is usually hard, the authors used the crowdsourcing platform CrowdFlower (CF).
A CF worker uses a chat-like interface for a three phase dialog about a randomly selected Simple questions BIBREF7 training example.
The described procedure leads to dialogs like the one shown in the Figure 2.
At the beginning, the system requests a paraphrase to familiarize the user with the question and obtain alternative wordings.
In the second phase, users provide explanations that must differ enough from the original question or be improved.
With a valid explanation, the last phase asks for a correct full-sentence answer, helping reveal cheaters and reject irrelevant answers.
Correct answers come from Simple questions as Freebase entities, and annotation determines whether dialogs contain consistent, other, or no answers.
The collection system needs to recognize following dialog acts from user utterances during all phases of the dialog.
One dialog act is that the user does not want to provide requested information.
One dialog act is that the user agrees to provide requested information.
One dialog act is that the user does not know the requested information.
One dialog act is that the user tries chit chat with the system, such as hello, bye, or who are you.
None of the above is interpreted as the user giving information requested by the system.
Dialog acts are parsed by hand written rules using templates and keyword spotting collected from frequent CF worker expressions.
The dataset contains 1900 dialogs and 8533 turns, with questions and correct Freebase entity answers from Simple questions BIBREF7.
The dataset consists of a standard data split into training, development and test files.
Each file contains complete dialogs enriched by NLU outputs, correct answers, and expert annotation of user answer hints.
351 dialogs contain correct user answers, 702 have incorrect answers, 847 have no answer, and dialogs contain 1828 paraphrases and 1539 explanations for 1870 questions.
Answers were labeled correct only when pointing to the same Freebase entity as Simple questions, and 285 incorrect answers were for general questions.
Training dialogs support feature extraction and engineering, while labeled validation data supports parameter tuning for interactive learning models.
Two proposed evaluation metrics score required information and answer extraction accuracy, with answers based only on training and seen testing dialogs.
The simulation evaluates how efficiently a dialog system uses user information while maximizing correctly answered questions and limiting requests.
The proposed evaluation measure is S_D = (n_c - w_i n_i - w_e n_e - w_a n_a)/|D| (Eq. 20).
In Eq. 20, n_c, n_i, n_e, n_a, and |D| denote counts, while w_i, w_e, and w_a are penalization weights.
Penalization weights compensate for different costs of obtaining information, with broader explanations relatively simple and correct answers significantly more difficult.
The authors recommend using their included evaluation scripts with penalization weights to make evaluations comparable between different systems.
Incorrect answers are penalized significantly.
Explanations are quite cheap and therefore penalized just slightly.
Gaining a question’s answer from users is harder than gaining explanations.
Answer Extraction Accuracy measures how often a correct answer is extracted from user answer hints in dialogs annotated as correctly answered.
Future work focuses on a baseline interactive learning system, dialog management improvements, and improving Simple question dataset accuracy using collected dialogs.
The paper presents evaluation of interactive learning approaches covering efficiency of using user information and accuracy on answer hints understanding.
The authors collected CrowdFlower conversational dialogs, annotated them with experts, published them under Creative Commons 4.0 BY-SA on lindat, and provide evaluation scripts.
The work was funded by LK11221, SVV project 260 224, GAUK grant 1170516, and used LINDAT/CLARIN resources under LM2015071.
